meta.title: Food Poisoning Chatbot Dataset
meta.description: Comprehensive dataset on food poisoning with proper intent detection. Emergency responses are triggered ONLY when the user explicitly states a personal crisis — not for general informational queries.
meta.intent_detection_note: The chatbot must classify user intent BEFORE responding. General symptom/cause/treatment questions always get informational answers. Emergency escalation is reserved for explicit crisis statements only.

intent_classification.description: Classify every incoming message into one of these intents before generating a response.

INFORMATIONAL.description: User is asking a general knowledge question about food poisoning.
triggers: What are the symptoms of food poisoning?
How long does food poisoning last?
What are the treatments for food poisoning?
INFORMATIONAL.response_type: Factual, educational, friendly answer using dataset knowledge.

PERSONAL_CONCERN.description: User suspects they personally have food poisoning but is not in immediate danger.
triggers: I think I have food poisoning
I have diarrhea after eating out
PERSONAL_CONCERN.response_type: Empathetic, practical advice. Suggest home care. Recommend seeing a doctor if symptoms are severe or prolonged.

MEDICAL_EMERGENCY.description: User explicitly states a life-threatening situation requiring immediate help.

intent_classification.critical_rule: NEVER trigger an emergency response for informational or educational questions. The words 'food poisoning', 'symptoms', 'vomiting', 'diarrhea' alone do NOT constitute an emergency.

system_prompt_template.description: Use this as the base system prompt for your chatbot.
system_prompt_template.prompt:
You are a helpful food safety and health information assistant. Your role is to provide clear, accurate, and educational information about food poisoning, foodborne illnesses, symptoms, causes, prevention, and treatment.

IMPORTANT RULES:
1. For general questions about symptoms, causes, treatment, or prevention — always answer informatively and helpfully.
2. Only trigger emergency guidance if the user EXPLICITLY states they or someone nearby is currently in a life-threatening situation (e.g., unconscious, unable to breathe, collapsing).
3. Never escalate to emergency mode for educational or general health questions.
4. If a user seems personally unwell but not in crisis, give practical advice and suggest consulting a doctor if symptoms are severe or persistent.
5. Always be friendly, calm, and factual.

informational_response.format: Answer directly and factually. Use clear sections if needed. End with a helpful follow-up offer.
informational_response.example_trigger: What are the symptoms of food poisoning?
informational_response.example_response: Food poisoning commonly causes: nausea and vomiting, diarrhea (sometimes bloody), abdominal pain and cramps, fever, headache, and fatigue. Symptoms usually start within a few hours to a few days after eating contaminated food and typically resolve within 1–3 days. Would you like to know about causes, treatment, or when to see a doctor?

personal_concern_response.format: Acknowledge concern, give practical home care advice, mention when to see a doctor.
personal_concern_response.example_trigger: I think I have food poisoning
personal_concern_response.example_response: I'm sorry you're feeling unwell. If you suspect food poisoning, the most important thing is to stay hydrated — sip water or an oral rehydration solution frequently. Rest and avoid solid food until vomiting settles, then try bland foods like toast or rice. See a doctor if you have a high fever, blood in your stool, diarrhea lasting more than 3 days, or signs of severe dehydration.

emergency_response.format: Only shown when user explicitly describes a life-threatening situation.
emergency_response.example_trigger: I can't breathe and I think I swallowed something poisonous
emergency_response.example_response:
This sounds like a medical emergency. Please call emergency services immediately:
🇮🇳 India: Ambulance → 108 | General Emergency → 112
🌍 International: Your local emergency number

While waiting for help: keep the person calm, do not give food or water, and stay on the line with emergency services.

overview.definition: Food poisoning (also called foodborne illness) is an infection or irritation of the digestive tract caused by consuming food or drinks contaminated with harmful bacteria, viruses, parasites, or toxins.
overview.typical_course: Most cases are acute (sudden onset, short duration), lasting less than a week and resolving without treatment.
overview.global_burden: The WHO estimates 600 million people fall ill from contaminated food each year, resulting in approximately 420,000 deaths annually.
overview.us_burden: About 48 million cases and 3,000 deaths annually in the United States.

symptoms.onset: Symptoms can begin 30 minutes to several weeks after eating contaminated food, depending on the pathogen.
symptoms.duration: Most mild cases resolve within 1–3 days. Severe infections may last a week or longer.

nervous_system_symptoms.description: Seen in serious cases such as botulism or shellfish poisoning.
nervous_system_symptoms.action: If nervous system symptoms occur, seek medical attention promptly.

adults: More than 6 loose stools in one day
when_to_see_doctor.note: Pregnant women, elderly adults, and immunocompromised individuals should consult a doctor earlier than otherwise healthy adults.

bacteria.name: E. coli (O157:H7)
bacteria.serious_complication: Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS) — kidney failure, especially in children

bacteria.name: Listeria monocytogenes
bacteria.note: Can grow in refrigerator. Can cause miscarriage or stillbirth in pregnant women.

bacteria.name: Staphylococcus aureus
bacteria.note: Toxin is heat-stable — reheating does not make contaminated food safe.

viruses.name: Norovirus
viruses.note: Most common cause of foodborne illness worldwide.

parasites.name: Cryptosporidium
parasites.note: Resistant to chlorine. Dangerous in immunocompromised individuals.

parasites.name: Toxoplasma gondii
parasites.note: Dangerous during pregnancy — can cause congenital defects.

toxins_and_chemicals.name: Staphylococcal enterotoxin
toxins_and_chemicals.note: Heat-stable toxin. Reheating food does NOT destroy it.

toxins_and_chemicals.name: Botulinum toxin
toxins_and_chemicals.note: Most potent natural toxin. Causes paralysis. Medical emergency.

toxins_and_chemicals.name: Pesticide residues
sources: Unwashed produce with excessive pesticide application

high_risk_foods: Raw or undercooked poultry and meat
Raw or undercooked seafood and shellfish
Cooked rice left at room temperature
risk_groups: People with chronic illnesses (diabetes, kidney disease, liver disease)

complications.common: Dehydration — the most frequent complication. Loss of fluids and electrolytes from vomiting and diarrhea.

serious.name: Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS)
serious.description: Destroys red blood cells and damages kidneys. Can cause acute kidney failure.

serious.name: Guillain-Barré Syndrome
serious.description: Immune system attacks nerves. Can cause paralysis.

serious.name: Reactive Arthritis
serious.description: Joint pain and inflammation following infection.

serious.name: Pregnancy complications
serious.description: Miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm labour, or severe neonatal illness.

serious.name: Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS)
serious.description: Can develop after severe foodborne infections.

home_care.most_important: Rehydration — replace lost fluids and electrolytes.
home_care.fluids_for_children: Oral rehydration solution (Pedialyte or equivalent). Infants should continue breast milk or formula.
foods_to_avoid: Dairy products (temporary lactose intolerance may occur)

antidiarrheal.caution: Do NOT use if you have bloody diarrhea or high fever. Do NOT give to children without medical advice.

antibiotics.note: Not required for most cases. Only prescribed by a doctor for specific severe bacterial infections.

medications.probiotics: May help shorten diarrhea duration. Consult a doctor before use.

hospital_care: Treatment for HUS or other serious complications

clean: Wash hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds before and after handling food
Wash all fruits and vegetables under running water
Sanitize cutting boards, utensils, and surfaces after each use
separate: Keep raw meat, poultry, seafood, and eggs away from ready-to-eat foods
Use separate cutting boards for raw meat and vegetables
Never reuse marinade from raw meat without boiling it first
cook: Cook poultry to internal temperature of 74°C (165°F)
Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb to 63°C (145°F)
Use a food thermometer — do not rely on colour alone
chill: Refrigerate perishable foods within 2 hours (1 hour if temperature is above 32°C)
Thaw food safely: in refrigerator, cold water, or microwave — never at room temperature
Do not leave food in the temperature danger zone: 5°C–60°C (40°F–140°F)
additional: Avoid unpasteurized milk, cheese, and juices
Watch for food recalls and discard recalled items
Do not feed honey to infants under 12 months (risk of infant botulism)
travelers_diarrhea_prevention: Drink only bottled or treated water
Avoid ice made from tap water
Avoid street food and raw/undercooked meat or seafood
Eat food that is served hot

safe_cooking_temperatures.eggs: Cook until yolk and white are firm

food_storage_guidelines.danger_zone: 5°C – 60°C (40°F – 140°F) — bacteria multiply rapidly in this range
food_storage_guidelines.note: Freezing stops bacterial growth but does not kill bacteria. Always reheat leftovers to 74°C before eating.

typhoid_fever.transmission: Fecal-oral route via contaminated food or water

diagnosis.clinical: Doctors often diagnose based on symptoms alone for mild, short-lasting cases.
medical_history_questions: What symptoms do you have and how long?
What foods or drinks did you consume recently?
Has anyone else who ate the same food fallen ill?
Do you have underlying health conditions or take medications?

tests.stool_culture: Identifies bacteria or parasites causing infection.
tests.blood_tests: Detects signs of infection or complications like dehydration.
tests.PCR: Molecular testing for rapid pathogen identification in advanced settings.

myths_and_facts.myth: You can tell if food is contaminated by its smell or appearance.
myths_and_facts.fact: Many dangerous bacteria (like Salmonella and E. coli) do not change the taste, smell, or look of food. When in doubt, throw it out.

myths_and_facts.myth: Reheating food always makes it safe.
myths_and_facts.fact: Reheating kills bacteria but does NOT destroy heat-stable toxins from Staphylococcus aureus or Bacillus cereus. Improperly stored food can still cause illness after reheating.
Drinking alcohol does not kill foodborne bacteria. The concentration consumed is far too low to have any antibacterial effect in the digestive system.

myths_and_facts.myth: Lemon juice or vinegar makes raw food safe.
myths_and_facts.fact: Acidic ingredients slow bacterial growth but do not reliably kill all pathogens. Raw fish marinated in citrus (ceviche) still carries risk.
Freezing stops bacteria from multiplying but does not kill them. Bacteria become active again when food thaws.

myths_and_facts.myth: Food poisoning always comes from the last meal you ate.
myths_and_facts.fact: Some pathogens like Listeria and Hepatitis A have incubation periods of weeks. The meal that caused illness may have been consumed days or weeks earlier.

faq.question: What is food poisoning?
faq.answer: Food poisoning (also called foodborne illness) is a sickness caused by eating food or drinking water contaminated with harmful bacteria, viruses, parasites, or toxins. It typically causes stomach upset, vomiting, and diarrhea.

faq.question: What are the symptoms of food poisoning?
faq.answer: Common symptoms include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea (sometimes bloody), abdominal cramps, fever, headache, and fatigue. Symptoms range from mild to severe and may last from a few hours to several days.

faq.question: How soon do symptoms start after eating contaminated food?
faq.answer: Onset varies by pathogen: Staphylococcus toxins cause symptoms within 30 minutes to 6 hours; Salmonella takes 6–48 hours; E. coli 3–4 days; Listeria 1–4 weeks. Most common cases begin within 2–6 hours.

faq.question: How long does food poisoning last?
faq.answer: Most mild to moderate cases resolve within 1–3 days. Serious infections like Listeria or E. coli O157:H7 can last a week or longer and may require medical treatment.

faq.question: What causes food poisoning?
faq.answer: Food poisoning is most commonly caused by bacteria (Salmonella, E. coli, Listeria, Campylobacter), viruses (norovirus, hepatitis A), parasites (Giardia, Cryptosporidium), and toxins from bacteria or naturally occurring in certain foods.

faq.question: How is food poisoning treated at home?
faq.answer: The most important step is replacing lost fluids. Drink water, oral rehydration solutions, clear broths, or diluted juice. Rest and avoid solid food until vomiting settles, then try bland foods like toast, rice, and bananas. Avoid dairy, caffeine, and fatty foods during recovery.

faq.question: When should I see a doctor?
faq.answer: See a doctor if you have a high fever, bloody stools, diarrhea lasting more than 3 days, signs of severe dehydration, nervous system symptoms, or if the affected person is an infant, elderly, pregnant, or immunocompromised.

faq.question: How can I prevent food poisoning?
faq.answer: Follow the 4 core principles: Clean (wash hands and surfaces), Separate (keep raw and cooked foods apart), Cook (to safe internal temperatures), and Chill (refrigerate promptly). Avoid unpasteurized products and raw/undercooked meat, eggs, and seafood.

faq.question: Is food poisoning contagious?
faq.answer: Some viral causes like norovirus and hepatitis A can spread person-to-person through poor hand hygiene. Most bacterial causes are not directly contagious but can spread through contaminated surfaces or shared food.

faq.question: What are the most dangerous complications of food poisoning?
faq.answer: The most dangerous complications include severe dehydration, hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS, which can cause kidney failure — especially in young children), botulism (paralysis), Guillain-Barré syndrome, and pregnancy complications such as miscarriage from Listeria.
